sections.news: BBL Injury News in South Florida
sections.faq: Common questions about BBL lawsuits in Florida

faq.q: How many BBL deaths have occurred in South Florida?
faq.a: A peer-reviewed study of South Florida counted 25 pulmonary-fat-embolism deaths linked to BBL procedures between January 2010 and April 2022, with six deaths in 2021 alone. See Pazmiño et al., Aesthetic Surgery Journal (PMC9896146) and Florida Senate staff analyses of HB 1561.

faq.q: Can you sue for a botched Brazilian butt lift in Miami?
faq.a: Florida medical-malpractice and wrongful-death lawsuits over BBL injuries are filed in state circuit courts (for example Miami-Dade). Public complaints allege nerve damage, infection, organ puncture, and fatal pulmonary fat embolism. This site lists indexed cases and news—it does not provide legal advice.

faq.q: What is the main medical risk that kills BBL patients?
faq.a: Pulmonary fat embolism (PFE) is the leading fatal complication when fat enters the bloodstream during gluteal fat grafting. Florida administrative rules restrict intramuscular gluteal injection (Rule 64B8-9.009).

faq.q: Are medspa BBL surgeries legal in Florida?
faq.a: Licensed physicians may perform cosmetic surgery in approved office settings, but facilities must meet Florida Department of Health rules. Lawsuits allege misleading credentials, high daily surgery volume, and failure to warn of BBL risks.

faq.q: Where can I find public BBL lawsuit dockets in Florida?
faq.a: Use county clerk portals (Miami-Dade OCS for South Florida), federal PACER/CourtListener for U.S. district cases, and Board of Medicine orders. This site summarizes publicly reported filings with links to primary sources.

sourcing: Florida state trial courts publish filings through county clerks (Miami-Dade OCS, Orange County, etc.).
Federal courts: PACER / CourtListener RECAP for U.S. District and Bankruptcy filings.
Florida Board of Medicine emergency orders and Florida Administrative Code 64B8-9.009 (gluteal fat grafting standards).
News articles link to primary reporting; they are not substitutes for reading the complaint.
Third-party docket aggregators (UniCourt, PacerMonitor) summarize public indices; verify case numbers with the official clerk before citing in court.
